children: Chicago wheat futures tumbled on Thursday, retreating from multi-year highs set this week and nearing the lower limit after Russian President Vladimir Putin said there was a chance of a peace agreement to end the war in Ukraine.

Traders said Putin's remarks triggered profit-taking after a steep rally in the past month linked to mounting concerns about the war disrupting crucial Black Sea grain exports from Russia and Ukraine.
on the Chicago Board of Trade was last down 28 cents to $7.46 a bushel as of 10:20 a.m. CT (1520 GMT).

"The Putin comment is short-term bullish, but with that said, the grains complex is in overbought territory and was looking for a reason for a selloff," said Mark Schultz, co-founder and CEO of Northstar Commodity.
The benchmark hit its highest since February 2023 on Wednesday at $7.95 a bushel, building on a 21% monthly rise in August.

Putin told an economic forum in Russia's Far East there was a chance of a peace agreement in Ukraine, but restarting talks was harder because of Ukrainian attacks on shipping and a call by Kyiv for civilian aircraft to avoid Russian airspace.
Some traders cautioned that Putin's remarks did not suggest an immediate prospect of military de-escalation and that physical disruption to Black Sea grain flows was unchanged.
Ukraine's combined grain and oilseed exports fell to 1.2 million metric tons in August from 2.5 million tons in July, Ukrainian traders union UGA said on Thursday.
Traders are watching to see how suppliers will approach a wheat import tender announced on Thursday by Saudi Arabia, for which Russia is a regular supplier.

The corn market has been supported since last month by falling expectations for U.S. harvest yields, while soybeans have been boosted by a run of Chinese purchases.
